RBC.desc: Red Blood Cell count, the number of oxygen-carrying cells per microliter of blood.
RBC.why: Screens for anemia (too few) and polycythemia (too many). Always read together with Hemoglobin and Hematocrit.
RBC.highMeans: A high count is most often from dehydration, living at altitude, smoking, or sleep apnea. Rarely, it points to a bone-marrow condition called polycythemia.
RBC.lowMeans: A low count suggests anemia. Common causes are iron deficiency, recent blood loss, low B12 or folate, or chronic inflammation.
RBC.context: Hydration status matters. Getting blood drawn dehydrated can artificially raise this number.

high: Hydrate consistently through the day, mild dehydration artificially lifts this number
If you smoke, quit, smoking thickens the blood
Address sleep apnea if you snore heavily or wake unrefreshed
low: Add iron-rich foods like red meat, lentils, spinach, and pair them with vitamin C to absorb better
Make sure you are getting enough B12 and folate from eggs, dairy, fish, and leafy greens
Avoid tea and coffee within an hour of iron-rich meals, tannins block absorption
maintain: Iron, B12, and folate adequate. Stay hydrated.

Hemoglobin.desc: The iron-containing protein inside red blood cells that actually carries oxygen to your tissues.
Hemoglobin.why: The primary number doctors use to diagnose anemia and track its severity.
Hemoglobin.highMeans: Elevated hemoglobin usually reflects dehydration, smoking, chronic lung issues, high altitude, or sleep apnea.
Hemoglobin.lowMeans: Low hemoglobin is the definition of anemia. Most common causes are iron deficiency, blood loss, B12/folate deficiency, kidney disease, or chronic inflammation.
Hemoglobin.context: A drop of more than 1 g/dL between tests is worth investigating even if the value is still in range.

high: Drink more water through the day, dehydration concentrates the blood
Quit smoking if relevant, it pushes hemoglobin up
If you live or train at altitude, that is a normal cause and is benign
low: Build up iron stores with red meat, lentils, beans, pumpkin seeds, and spinach
Pair iron foods with vitamin C sources like citrus or bell peppers to triple absorption
If periods are not the cause for you, rule out GI bleeding (stool occult blood test)
Consider a trial of iron supplementation if ferritin is also low
maintain: Iron 3 to 4 times per week (see iron and ferritin plan), B12 from animal foods or supplement, folate 400 mcg per day from leafy greens and beans.
Recheck CBC yearly.

Hematocrit.desc: The percentage of your blood that is made up of red blood cells (the rest is plasma and white cells).
Hematocrit.why: Cross-checks Hemoglobin and RBC. Useful for spotting dehydration (falsely high) or blood loss (falsely low).
Hematocrit.highMeans: High Hct usually means dehydration or the same things that raise Hemoglobin, smoking, altitude, sleep apnea, rarely polycythemia.
Hematocrit.lowMeans: Low Hct usually means anemia (too few red cells) or overhydration diluting the blood.
Hematocrit.context: Hct closely tracks Hemoglobin. Interpret them together, not independently.

high: Drink water consistently, this rises with dehydration
Cut back on alcohol, it dehydrates and irritates marrow
Quit smoking if relevant
low: Add iron-rich foods and pair with vitamin C
Check B12 and folate if vegetarian or vegan
Rule out chronic blood loss if the drop is unexplained
maintain: Hydrate consistently (2.5 to 3.5 L per day). Most hematocrit swings are hydration.
Iron and B12 sufficient as above.

MCV.desc: Mean Corpuscular Volume, the average size of your red blood cells.
MCV.why: Categorizes anemia by cell size: small (microcytic) often means iron deficiency, large (macrocytic) often means B12 or folate deficiency.
MCV.highMeans: Big red cells (macrocytic) most often point to B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol use, hypothyroidism, or certain medications.
MCV.lowMeans: Small red cells (microcytic) most often mean iron deficiency or thalassemia (a genetic trait common in Mediterranean populations).
MCV.context: MCV is the single best triage tool once anemia is confirmed.

high: Cut alcohol, heavy intake enlarges red cells
Eat more folate (leafy greens, legumes, fortified grains) and B12 (fish, meat, dairy)
Check thyroid if fatigue or cold intolerance are present
low: Boost iron intake with red meat, lentils, pumpkin seeds, plus vitamin C alongside
Skip tea or coffee at iron-rich meals
maintain: Maintain B12 (above 500 pg/mL) and folate (above 7 ng/mL).
Iron sufficient as above.

MCH.desc: Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin, the average amount of hemoglobin inside each red blood cell.
MCH.why: Supports MCV in classifying anemia. Low MCH almost always rides with low MCV and points to iron issues.
MCH.highMeans: Usually mirrors high MCV, B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism.
MCH.lowMeans: Usually mirrors low MCV, iron deficiency or thalassemia trait.
MCH.context: Interpret alongside MCV and MCHC, never in isolation.

high: Cut alcohol, add B12 and folate from fish, eggs, leafy greens
low: Build iron with red meat, lentils, dark greens plus vitamin C
maintain: Eat heme iron 3 to 4 times per week (4 to 6 oz red meat or dark poultry).
Get B12 from animal foods or 500 mcg methylcobalamin if vegetarian.
Get 400 mcg folate per day from leafy greens, beans, and fortified grains.

MCHC.desc: Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration, how densely packed the hemoglobin is inside each red cell.
MCHC.why: Helps separate iron-deficiency anemia from other types. Also a quality check for blood samples.
MCHC.highMeans: True elevations are rare; usually hereditary spherocytosis or a lab artifact from cold agglutinins.
MCHC.lowMeans: Low MCHC (hypochromic cells) points to iron deficiency anemia.
MCHC.context: If isolated and the rest of the CBC is normal, a mildly off MCHC often has no clinical meaning.

high: Usually a lab artifact, stay hydrated and retest if out of range
low: Focus on iron and vitamin C together at meals
maintain: Iron and hydration sufficient.

RDW-CV.desc: Red cell Distribution Width, how much variation there is in the size of your red blood cells.
RDW-CV.why: A rising RDW is an early signal that your marrow is making a mixed population of cells, often before anemia shows up.
RDW-CV.highMeans: A high RDW means your red cells are unusually varied in size. Commonly iron, B12, or folate deficiency starting to show.
RDW-CV.lowMeans: A low RDW is not clinically meaningful.
RDW-CV.context: RDW often rises before Hemoglobin drops, it's an early-warning marker for nutritional anemia.

high: Cover both iron (red meat, lentils, spinach) and B12 or folate (eggs, fish, greens)
Reduce alcohol, it is a common cause of mixed red cell populations
maintain: Iron, B12, and folate sufficient. RDW rises early in nutrient deficiencies.

Platelets.desc: The tiny cell fragments in blood that form clots when you're injured.
Platelets.why: Checks both bleeding risk (low) and clotting risk (high).
Platelets.highMeans: High platelets (thrombocytosis) are usually reactive, from inflammation, infection, iron deficiency, or recent intense exercise. Sustained highs can raise clot risk.
Platelets.lowMeans: Low platelets (thrombocytopenia) can be from a viral illness, certain medications, autoimmune conditions, or liver disease. Very low values raise bleeding risk.
Platelets.context: A single reading just below the reference range is usually not concerning. Trend over multiple tests matters more.

high: Add omega-3 from fatty fish twice a week to reduce stickiness
Limit processed foods and stay active, inflammation nudges platelets up
Quit smoking if relevant
low: Cut alcohol, even moderate intake can suppress platelets
Add folate and B12 from greens, beans, fish, and eggs
maintain: Hydrate, eat plenty of B12 and folate.
Avoid daily NSAIDs unless needed.
Recheck CBC yearly.

MPV.desc: Mean Platelet Volume, the average size of your platelets.
MPV.why: Helps distinguish whether platelet counts are changing due to production (young, bigger platelets) or destruction (older, mixed sizes).
MPV.highMeans: High MPV suggests your marrow is cranking out fresh, young platelets, common when platelets are being destroyed or consumed faster than normal.
MPV.lowMeans: Low MPV suggests reduced platelet production and can be seen in some marrow conditions or after chemotherapy.
MPV.context: MPV alone rarely drives decisions. Always interpret with platelet count.

high: Add omega-3, exercise regularly, and manage blood pressure
low: No specific lifestyle action, trend matters more than a single value
maintain: Usually no targeted action. Track with the rest of the platelet picture.

WBC.desc: White Blood Cell count, total immune cells in your blood.
WBC.why: Screens for infection (usually pushes it up), immune suppression (low), and blood cancers (very high or very low).
WBC.highMeans: A high WBC usually means infection, inflammation, recent intense exercise, or stress. Very high levels (>20k) need prompt workup.
WBC.lowMeans: A low WBC can be from viral infection, autoimmune conditions, certain medications, B12/folate deficiency, or less commonly a marrow problem.
WBC.context: Exercise in the hours before testing can transiently raise WBC. Avoid hard workouts the morning of a draw.

high: Prioritize 7 to 9 hours of sleep, poor sleep raises WBC
Manage stress with walks, breathwork, or meditation
Load up on anti-inflammatory foods, berries, olive oil, fatty fish, leafy greens
Quit smoking if relevant
low: Prioritize sleep and stress control, both suppress immune cell production
Get zinc from oysters, beef, pumpkin seeds, and vitamin D from sun or supplement
maintain: Sleep 7 to 9 hours. Sleep deprivation distorts WBC counts.
Train 150 min per week, eat Mediterranean style.
Recheck CBC yearly.

Neutrophils %.desc: The percentage of your white cells that are neutrophils, the first responders to bacterial infection.
Neutrophils %.why: Helps identify what kind of immune activity is happening. A high neutrophil fraction usually points to bacterial infection or inflammation.
Neutrophils %.highMeans: Elevated neutrophils point to bacterial infection, inflammation, stress, or recent steroid use.
Neutrophils %.lowMeans: Low neutrophils (neutropenia) raise infection risk and can come from viral illness, autoimmune disease, medications, or B12/folate deficiency.
Neutrophils %.context: Absolute neutrophil count matters more than the percentage, a high percentage with a normal WBC may not mean much.

high: Manage acute stress and inflammation, cut processed foods
Address smoking if relevant
low: Focus on sleep and stress, both drive this up
Ensure adequate vitamin B12, folate, and zinc
maintain: Address sources of chronic inflammation. Mediterranean diet, training, sleep, low alcohol.

Lymphocytes %.desc: The percentage of your white cells that are lymphocytes, the cells that handle viruses and long-term immunity.
Lymphocytes %.why: Patterns here suggest viral vs bacterial processes. A high lymphocyte fraction often reflects a viral illness.
Lymphocytes %.highMeans: High lymphocytes commonly follow a viral infection (mono, COVID, CMV). Persistent high levels need workup.
Lymphocytes %.lowMeans: Low lymphocytes can be from acute stress, corticosteroids, viral infection early on, chronic illness, or some immune conditions.
Lymphocytes %.context: Percentages shift whenever neutrophils shift, always check absolute counts if either side looks off.

high: Often reflects a viral exposure, rest and fluids usually settle it
low: Sleep 7 to 9 hours, chronic under-sleeping drops lymphocytes
Get vitamin D and zinc from sun, fish, oysters, seeds
Reduce chronic stress, cortisol suppresses lymphocytes
maintain: Sleep 7 to 9 hours. Lymphocyte function tracks tightly with sleep.
Sun exposure and vitamin D 40 to 60 ng/mL.
Manage chronic stress.

Monocytes %.desc: The percentage of white cells that are monocytes, the immune cells that clean up damaged tissue and fight chronic infections.
Monocytes %.why: Monocytosis can signal chronic inflammation, recovery from illness, or less commonly blood disorders.
Monocytes %.highMeans: High monocytes often reflect chronic inflammation, autoimmune disease, or recovery from an infection.
Monocytes %.lowMeans: Low monocytes are rarely clinically meaningful on their own.
Monocytes %.context: Small percentage changes in monocytes rarely matter by themselves.

high: Cut ultra-processed foods, add fatty fish and colorful vegetables
Exercise 150 minutes a week
low: Usually benign, focus on sleep and nutrition fundamentals
maintain: Mediterranean diet, regular training, sleep.

Eosinophils %.desc: White cells that respond mostly to parasites and allergic reactions.
Eosinophils %.why: Elevated eosinophils point toward allergy, asthma, parasitic infection, or drug reactions.
Eosinophils %.highMeans: High eosinophils commonly mean allergies, asthma, eczema, parasitic infection, or a drug reaction.
Eosinophils %.lowMeans: Low eosinophils are not clinically concerning and often follow stress or steroid use.
Eosinophils %.context: Eosinophils dip in acute stress and rise slowly, interpret trends, not single readings.

high: Identify and remove allergen triggers (pollens, dust, food)
Consider a deworming check if you have travel history
Add omega-3 to lower allergic inflammation
low: Usually benign and needs no action
maintain: Address allergies, parasites, or skin conditions if persistently elevated.
Mediterranean diet supports lower baseline eosinophils.

Basophils %.desc: The rarest white blood cell, involved in allergic and inflammatory responses.
Basophils %.why: Very small fraction of total WBCs. Rarely the primary driver of any diagnosis.
Basophils %.highMeans: Mild elevations can follow allergic reactions or chronic inflammation. Very high basophils are rare and may warrant further workup.
Basophils %.lowMeans: Low basophils are not clinically meaningful.
Basophils %.context: Measured as a percentage, so small absolute changes can look dramatic.

high: Usually allergy-related, identify triggers and add omega-3
low: Usually benign, no action needed
maintain: Usually a tiny fraction. No specific maintenance needed if other counts are normal.

ESR (1 hr).desc: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate, how fast red cells settle in a tube. A nonspecific marker of inflammation.
ESR (1 hr).why: Rises with chronic inflammation, infection, autoimmune disease, or certain cancers. Used to monitor inflammation over time.
ESR (1 hr).highMeans: A high ESR signals inflammation somewhere in the body but doesn't say where. Could be infection, autoimmune disease, tissue injury, or (uncommon) cancer.
ESR (1 hr).lowMeans: Low ESR is not a concern.
ESR (1 hr).context: Normal ESR rises gradually with age and is usually higher in women. Pair with hs-CRP for a fuller picture.

high: Eat Mediterranean style, lots of olive oil, fatty fish, nuts, leafy greens
Move 150 minutes a week, add 2 strength sessions
Drop 5 to 10 percent of body weight if overweight, fat tissue drives inflammation
Sleep 7 to 9 hours, short sleep keeps ESR elevated
Quit smoking and limit alcohol to 0 to 2 drinks a week
low: Low ESR is benign, no action
maintain: Drive inflammation down with diet and lifestyle. Mediterranean style eating, regular cardio, sleep, low alcohol.
If ESR is persistently elevated with normal CRP, ask about underlying autoimmune workup.

Glucose Fasting.desc: Blood sugar measured after an overnight fast (8-12 hours without food).
Glucose Fasting.why: Core screen for prediabetes and diabetes. Values 100-125 mg/dL are prediabetic; 126+ on two occasions is diabetes.
Glucose Fasting.highMeans: A high fasting glucose suggests insulin resistance or early diabetes. Even a single high reading deserves a retest plus HbA1c.
Glucose Fasting.lowMeans: Low fasting glucose (hypoglycemia) is unusual on a morning fast and may signal excess insulin, adrenal issues, or liver problems.
Glucose Fasting.context: Must be truly fasted. Coffee, gum, or stress can nudge it up. Prior-day carb intake also matters.

high: Cut refined carbs and sugary drinks, swap for whole grains, legumes, and vegetables
Eat protein and fiber first at each meal, it blunts the glucose spike
Walk 10 to 15 minutes after each main meal, muscles pull glucose out of the blood
Add 2 to 3 strength sessions a week, muscle improves glucose disposal
Sleep 7 to 9 hours, short sleep raises fasting glucose within days
If BMI is over 25, losing 5 to 10 percent of body weight can normalize this
low: Eat small, regular meals with protein and complex carbs
Avoid alcohol on an empty stomach, it drops glucose
maintain: Eat your last meal 3+ hours before bed. Late eating raises morning glucose.
Walk 10 to 15 minutes after each main meal.
Strength train 2 to 3 times per week.
Sleep 7 to 9 hours. Even one short night raises fasting glucose 5 to 10 mg/dL.
Hold fasting glucose under 95 mg/dL for healthspan, not just under 100.

HbA1c.desc: Hemoglobin A1c, your average blood sugar over the past 2-3 months, expressed as a percentage.
HbA1c.why: The most reliable measure of long-term blood sugar control. Less affected by yesterday's dinner than fasting glucose.
HbA1c.highMeans: 5.7-6.4% is prediabetic. 6.5%+ meets diabetes criteria. Each 0.1% change reflects real change in average glucose.
HbA1c.lowMeans: Very low HbA1c is unusual unless you've had significant blood loss, hemolysis, or a red-cell disorder that shortens red cell lifespan.
HbA1c.context: Conditions that shorten red cell life (hemolysis, iron deficiency anemia after repletion) can falsely lower HbA1c.

high: Cut added sugar and refined grains, replace with whole grains, legumes, vegetables, and berries
Walk 10 to 15 minutes after every meal, this flattens post-meal glucose
Do 2 to 3 strength workouts a week, muscle is your glucose sink
Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep, poor sleep raises insulin resistance
If you are carrying extra weight, a 5 to 7 percent loss typically drops A1c by 0.3 to 0.5 points
Keep alcohol at or under one drink a day
low: Very low A1c can reflect recent anemia, address iron and B12 status
maintain: Keep added sugar under 25 g per day. Replace sweet drinks with water, sparkling water, or unsweetened tea.
Anchor each meal with 25 to 35 g protein and 8 to 12 g fiber to flatten glucose spikes.
Walk 10 to 15 minutes within 30 minutes of finishing a meal. This drops post-meal glucose by 20 to 30 percent.
Strength train 2 to 3 times per week. Muscle is your largest glucose sink.
Sleep 7 to 9 hours. One night under 6 hours raises insulin resistance the next day by 30 percent.
Stay within 5 percent of optimal bodyweight.
Recheck HbA1c every 6 to 12 months. Target under 5.4 percent for healthspan, not just under 5.7.

Insulin.desc: The hormone that moves glucose from your blood into cells. Measured fasting.
Insulin.why: Tells you how hard your pancreas is working to keep glucose normal. High insulin with normal glucose = insulin resistance.
Insulin.highMeans: High fasting insulin points to insulin resistance, your cells are responding less to insulin, so your pancreas makes more.
Insulin.lowMeans: Low fasting insulin with normal glucose is usually fine. With high glucose, it may suggest reduced pancreatic output.
Insulin.context: Must be drawn fasting. Interpret alongside fasting glucose using HOMA-IR.

high: Shift to a lower-refined-carb, higher-fiber, higher-protein pattern
Post-meal walks and 2 to 3 strength sessions a week are very effective
Lose 5 to 10 percent of body weight if overweight, this often halves insulin
Prioritize sleep and reduce late-night eating
low: Pair carbs with protein and fat for steady energy, see MD if you feel hypoglycemic
maintain: Keep fasting insulin under 6 uIU/mL for optimal metabolic health.
Eat protein-forward (25 to 35 g) at each meal, with 8 to 12 g fiber. Limit liquid carbs.
Walk after meals, strength train 2 to 3 times per week.
If insulin creeps up, the earliest fix is usually fewer refined carbs and more daily steps (8000 to 10000).

HOMA-IR.desc: A calculated score combining fasting glucose and insulin to estimate insulin resistance.
HOMA-IR.why: Better early-warning sign of metabolic dysfunction than glucose alone. Below 2.0 is generally insulin sensitive.
HOMA-IR.highMeans: HOMA-IR above 2 suggests insulin resistance, even before fasting glucose or HbA1c go abnormal.
HOMA-IR.lowMeans: Low HOMA-IR indicates good insulin sensitivity, ideal.
HOMA-IR.context: Calculated from the same blood draw as fasting glucose and insulin, so both must be fasting.

high: Combine lower refined carbs, higher fiber, and at least 150 minutes of cardio plus 2 strength sessions a week
Target a 5 to 10 percent body-weight reduction if BMI is above 25
Sleep 7 to 9 hours and cap alcohol at one drink a day
low: This is favorable, keep the current routine
maintain: Target HOMA-IR under 1.0. Anything above 2 means insulin resistance is brewing.
Cut refined carbs, walk after meals, and strength train.
Drop bodyweight by 5 to 7 percent if you are above optimal. Even a small drop reverses insulin resistance fast.

Total Cholesterol.desc: The sum of all cholesterol in your blood (LDL + HDL + VLDL).
Total Cholesterol.why: Screening number for cardiovascular risk. Individual fractions (LDL, HDL) matter more.
Total Cholesterol.highMeans: High total cholesterol raises cardiovascular risk but the split between LDL and HDL is what really matters. High total with high HDL is less concerning than high total with high LDL.
Total Cholesterol.lowMeans: Very low total cholesterol is uncommon and usually incidental.
Total Cholesterol.context: Must be drawn fasting (9-12 hours) for an accurate LDL calculation.

high: Cut saturated fat, butter, fatty cuts of meat, full-fat cheese, tropical oils
Add 25 to 35 g of fiber a day, oats, beans, lentils, chia, vegetables
Eat fatty fish twice a week or take 1 to 2 g of EPA or DHA daily
Swap butter and coconut oil for olive oil and nuts
Exercise 30 to 45 minutes most days, this lifts HDL and shifts particles favorably
If overweight, drop 5 to 10 percent of body weight
low: Very low total cholesterol can signal malabsorption, focus on a varied diet with healthy fats
maintain: Follow the LDL maintenance program. Total cholesterol moves with LDL.
Get 30 to 40 g fiber per day with 5 to 10 g viscous fiber.
Use olive oil, eat fish 2x weekly, train 150 min per week.

HDL Cholesterol.desc: High-Density Lipoprotein, the 'good' cholesterol that carries excess cholesterol back to the liver for disposal.
HDL Cholesterol.why: Higher HDL is protective against cardiovascular disease. Below 40 mg/dL is a risk factor.
HDL Cholesterol.highMeans: High HDL (>60 mg/dL) is generally favorable and associated with lower heart disease risk.
HDL Cholesterol.lowMeans: Low HDL (<40 mg/dL) is a cardiovascular risk factor. Commonly seen with metabolic syndrome, sedentary lifestyle, smoking, or very low-fat diets.
HDL Cholesterol.context: Exercise and olive oil raise HDL. Extreme keto can temporarily lower it. Hormonal changes matter too.

high: Very high HDL is usually fine, keep the healthy habits that got you there
low: Do aerobic exercise at moderate intensity 150 to 200 minutes a week, this raises HDL most reliably
Add monounsaturated fats, olive oil, avocado, almonds, pistachios
Eat fatty fish twice a week for omega-3
Quit smoking, it drops HDL meaningfully
Lose 5 to 10 percent of body weight if relevant, HDL rises with weight loss
Limit refined carbs and sugar, they lower HDL
maintain: Train aerobically 150 to 250 min per week at zone 2 (you can hold a sentence). HDL responds to volume.
Add 2 strength sessions weekly. Resistance work raises HDL by 5 to 10 percent.
Use extra virgin olive oil as your primary fat. 2 to 3 tbsp per day.
Eat fatty fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel) 2 to 3 times per week for omega-3s.
Eat a handful of nuts daily (almonds, walnuts, pistachios). 1 oz, about 23 almonds.
Keep alcohol to 0 to 7 drinks per week. More than that hurts more than it helps.
Maintain bodyweight within 5 percent of optimal. Each kg lost raises HDL ~0.4 mg/dL.

LDL Cholesterol.desc: Low-Density Lipoprotein, the 'bad' cholesterol that can deposit in artery walls and form plaque.
LDL Cholesterol.why: LDL is the primary target for cardiovascular risk reduction. Lower is better for most adults.
LDL Cholesterol.highMeans: High LDL raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. Diet and genetics both contribute. Optimal is <100 mg/dL; <70 for anyone with existing heart disease.
LDL Cholesterol.lowMeans: Very low LDL (<40 mg/dL) without medication is uncommon. Usually fine but worth noting with your doctor.
LDL Cholesterol.context: Most labs calculate LDL from other lipids. Accurate calculation requires fasting. Direct LDL-C is more reliable when triglycerides are high.

high: Replace saturated fat (red meat, butter, cheese, palm oil) with olive oil, avocado, nuts
Eat 5 to 10 g of soluble fiber daily, oats, barley, beans, apples, psyllium
Add plant sterols (2 g a day) from fortified foods or supplements
Eat fatty fish twice a week or take 1 to 2 g EPA or DHA
Exercise 30 to 45 minutes most days
Drop 5 to 10 percent body weight if overweight
low: Low LDL is usually favorable, no action
maintain: Cap saturated fat at under 10 percent of calories. For 2500 kcal that is ~28 g per day. Watch butter, full-fat dairy, fatty cuts of beef.
Eat 30 to 40 g of fiber daily, with 5 to 10 g viscous fiber (oats, barley, beans, psyllium husk 1 to 2 tbsp).
Use plant sterols 2 g per day (fortified spread or supplement) for an additional 8 to 10 percent LDL drop.
Cook with olive, avocado, or canola oil. Drop coconut oil and palm oil.
Eat 4 to 5 oz fatty fish 2 times per week for omega-3.
150 min cardio per week plus 2 strength sessions.
Recheck full lipid panel plus ApoB yearly. ApoB is the better risk number.

Triglycerides.desc: The form of fat that travels through your blood. Mostly come from dietary carbohydrates and alcohol, not from dietary fat.
Triglycerides.why: High triglycerides are part of metabolic syndrome and an independent heart-disease risk. Very high (>500) raises pancreatitis risk.
Triglycerides.highMeans: Elevated triglycerides usually reflect too much refined carbs, sugar, or alcohol, or underlying insulin resistance.
Triglycerides.context: Strictly fasting (no food 9-12 hours). A big dinner the night before can dramatically raise the reading.

high: Cut sugar and refined carbs, sodas, sweets, white bread, these are the main driver
Limit alcohol to 0 to 3 drinks a week, alcohol is a strong triglyceride pusher
Eat fatty fish twice a week or take 2 to 4 g of EPA or DHA daily under guidance
Do 150 minutes of cardio a week
Lose 5 to 10 percent body weight if overweight
low: Low triglycerides are favorable, no action
maintain: Cap added sugar under 25 g per day. Watch fruit juice, soda, sweetened coffee, sauces, dressings.
Limit refined carbs (white bread, white rice, pastries) to less than 1 serving per day.
Keep alcohol to less than 5 drinks per week. Alcohol triples liver triglyceride production.
Eat fatty fish 2 to 3 times per week. EPA + DHA total 2 g daily can drop triglycerides 20 to 30 percent.
Walk 10 to 15 minutes after main meals.
150 min zone 2 cardio per week plus 2 strength sessions.
Aim for fasting triglycerides under 100 mg/dL. The lab 'normal' of under 150 is too lax.

VLDL.desc: Very Low-Density Lipoprotein, particles that carry triglycerides from the liver into the blood.
VLDL.why: A secondary cholesterol marker. Moves in the same direction as triglycerides and adds a bit of cardiovascular risk.
VLDL.highMeans: High VLDL usually tracks with high triglycerides and points to the same issues: too much refined carb or alcohol, or insulin resistance.
VLDL.lowMeans: Low VLDL is not a concern.
VLDL.context: Calculated from triglycerides in most labs (Trig ÷ 5). Treat the same way as triglycerides.

high: Cut sugar, refined carbs, and alcohol
Add omega-3 from fish or supplement
Exercise 150 minutes a week and lose weight if overweight
low: Low is favorable
maintain: VLDL tracks triglycerides. Keep added sugar low, alcohol low, train 150 min per week.
Eat fish twice per week or take 2 g EPA+DHA fish oil daily.

Non-HDL Cholesterol.desc: Total cholesterol minus HDL, all the 'bad' cholesterol fractions combined.
Non-HDL Cholesterol.why: A better predictor of cardiovascular risk than LDL alone, especially when triglycerides are high.
Non-HDL Cholesterol.highMeans: High non-HDL means your LDL + VLDL + other atherogenic particles are raised. Aim for <130; <100 if you have other risk factors.
Non-HDL Cholesterol.context: Non-HDL is accurate whether you're fasting or not, useful when someone forgets to fast.

high: Same playbook as LDL, less saturated fat, more soluble fiber, fatty fish, exercise, weight loss
low: Low is favorable
maintain: Drive non-HDL by lowering LDL and triglycerides. Follow the LDL and triglyceride playbooks.
Aim for non-HDL under 130 mg/dL, ideally under 100 if you have any cardiac risk.
Track ApoB yearly alongside non-HDL.

Total Chol/HDL Ratio.desc: Total Cholesterol divided by HDL. A single number for cardiovascular risk.
Total Chol/HDL Ratio.why: Captures how well-balanced your lipid profile is. Ideal is under 3.5; above 5 raises risk.
Total Chol/HDL Ratio.highMeans: A high ratio means either total cholesterol is too high, HDL is too low, or both. Below 4.5 is generally the target.
Total Chol/HDL Ratio.context: Harder to move than individual lipids, best improved by raising HDL (exercise) while lowering LDL (diet).

high: Raise HDL with aerobic exercise, olive oil, nuts, fish, and by quitting smoking
Lower LDL with soluble fiber and less saturated fat
Lose 5 to 10 percent body weight if relevant
low: Low ratio is ideal
maintain: Same playbook as LDL/HDL. Cardio 150 min per week, strength 2x per week, fiber 30 to 40 g per day.
Target under 3.5.

LDL/HDL Ratio.desc: LDL divided by HDL. Another ratio for cardiovascular risk.
LDL/HDL Ratio.why: Useful secondary marker. Under 3.5 is generally good; under 2.5 is excellent.
LDL/HDL Ratio.highMeans: A high ratio means LDL is outpacing HDL. Treat the same way as high LDL + low HDL: diet, exercise, and potentially medication.
LDL/HDL Ratio.context: Track with Total Chol/HDL ratio; they move together.

high: Raise HDL, exercise, olive oil, nuts, fatty fish, no smoking
Lower LDL, fiber, less saturated fat, weight loss if relevant
low: Low ratio is ideal
maintain: Drive both sides. Lower LDL with fiber and saturated fat reduction, raise HDL with cardio and olive oil.
Target ratio under 2.0 for active adults.

sdLDL Cholesterol.desc: Small, dense LDL particles, the most atherogenic LDL subtype that squeezes into artery walls.
sdLDL Cholesterol.why: A more refined cardiovascular risk marker than standard LDL. Elevated sdLDL is strongly linked to metabolic syndrome and heart disease.
sdLDL Cholesterol.highMeans: High sdLDL points to insulin resistance, high triglycerides, and low HDL, the classic metabolic syndrome pattern. These particles form plaque more aggressively than large LDL.
sdLDL Cholesterol.context: Not part of standard lipid panels in most labs. Test if you have high triglycerides, low HDL, or family history of heart disease.

high: Cut refined carbs and sugar, they drive small dense LDL specifically
Exercise 150 minutes a week plus 2 strength sessions
Lose 5 to 10 percent body weight if overweight
Add omega-3 from fatty fish twice a week
low: Low small dense LDL is favorable
maintain: Small dense LDL responds best to lowering triglycerides. Cut sugar, refined carbs, and alcohol.
Aim triglycerides under 100 and the small LDL fraction shrinks.
Strength train 2 to 3 times per week and walk after meals.

Creatinine.desc: A waste product from normal muscle breakdown that your kidneys filter out.
Creatinine.why: The standard marker of kidney function. Rising creatinine means your kidneys are filtering less.
Creatinine.highMeans: High creatinine points to reduced kidney function, dehydration, or high muscle mass (athletes often run a bit high). Persistent elevation deserves workup.
Creatinine.lowMeans: Low creatinine can be from low muscle mass, pregnancy, or overhydration before the test.
Creatinine.context: Well-muscled people naturally run higher. Intense exercise in the 24 hours before testing can also raise it temporarily.

high: Drink water through the day, chronic mild dehydration raises creatinine
Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) for routine aches, they stress the kidney
Keep blood pressure at or under 120 over 80
Moderate protein to about 0.8 to 1.0 g per kg body weight if kidney function is borderline
If you take creatine supplements, hold them for 3 to 4 weeks before retesting
low: Low creatinine is usually fine, especially with low muscle mass, add strength training
maintain: Drink 2.5 to 3.5 L water per day depending on size and activity.
Cap creatine supplementation to 3 to 5 g per day if you use it. It raises serum creatinine without harming kidneys.
Limit NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) to occasional use. Daily NSAIDs damage kidneys.
Keep blood pressure under 120/80 and HbA1c under 5.7. These are the top two kidney protectors.
Recheck creatinine and eGFR yearly.

eGFR.desc: Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate, how much blood your kidneys filter per minute, calculated from creatinine.
eGFR.why: The primary number used to stage kidney health. Above 90 is normal; 60-89 is mildly reduced; below 60 for 3+ months is chronic kidney disease.
eGFR.highMeans: Very high eGFR (>120) is usually fine and reflects excellent kidney function or low muscle mass.
eGFR.lowMeans: Below 60 suggests reduced kidney function. Below 30 is severe and needs specialist care.
eGFR.context: eGFR naturally declines with age (about 1 mL/min/year after 40). A trend downward matters more than a single value.

high: Very high GFR is usually benign in younger, lean adults
low: Keep blood pressure at or under 120 over 80 and blood sugar tight
Avoid routine NSAIDs, switch to paracetamol for occasional pain
Moderate protein intake, 0.8 g per kg body weight
Stay well hydrated and limit salt to under 5 g a day
Do not smoke
maintain: Stay hydrated, control blood pressure under 120/80, keep HbA1c under 5.7.
Avoid daily NSAIDs and excessive protein loading above 2.2 g/kg/day if eGFR is borderline.
Recheck yearly. If trending down, also order cystatin C eGFR for a more accurate read.

BUN/Urea.desc: Blood Urea Nitrogen, the nitrogen portion of urea, a waste product from protein breakdown cleared by the kidneys.
BUN/Urea.why: Secondary kidney function marker. Also shifts with hydration and protein intake.
BUN/Urea.highMeans: High BUN is most often dehydration or a high-protein meal. Can also reflect GI bleeding, kidney dysfunction, or heart failure.
BUN/Urea.lowMeans: Low BUN can mean liver disease, low-protein diet, or overhydration.
BUN/Urea.context: Rises quickly with dehydration. Drink water and retest before jumping to conclusions.

high: Drink more water, dehydration is the top cause of mildly elevated BUN
Ease up on very high protein intakes (over 2 g per kg) if kidney function is borderline
low: Usually benign, can reflect low protein or liver adjustment, keep protein at 1 g per kg
maintain: Stay well hydrated. Most BUN swings are dehydration.
Distribute protein across the day (25 to 40 g per meal) rather than mega-doses.
Limit alcohol and NSAID use.

BUN/Creat Ratio.desc: BUN divided by Creatinine. Helps distinguish dehydration from actual kidney issues.
BUN/Creat Ratio.why: A ratio >20 suggests dehydration or GI bleeding. Ratio 10-20 is normal. Below 10 may point to liver disease or low protein intake.
BUN/Creat Ratio.highMeans: High ratio is usually dehydration. Persistent high ratios can suggest upper GI bleeding or heart failure.
BUN/Creat Ratio.lowMeans: Low ratio can reflect liver disease, low-protein diet, or pregnancy.
BUN/Creat Ratio.context: A practical triage tool when both BUN and creatinine look off.

high: Usually a hydration signal, drink water steadily
Check for GI bleeding only if there are symptoms
low: Usually benign, ensure adequate protein intake
maintain: Hydrate consistently. Most ratio shifts are hydration not pathology.

Uric Acid.desc: A waste product from breakdown of purines (found in meat, seafood, beer, and sugar).
Uric Acid.why: Elevated uric acid causes gout and contributes to kidney stones. Also linked to metabolic syndrome.
Uric Acid.highMeans: High uric acid raises the risk of gout attacks and kidney stones. Driven by red meat, seafood, beer, fructose-sweetened drinks, and sometimes kidney issues.
Uric Acid.lowMeans: Very low uric acid is uncommon and usually benign.
Uric Acid.context: Dehydration and fasting raise uric acid. Rapid weight loss (especially keto) can trigger a flare.

high: Cut alcohol especially beer, it drives uric acid up fast
Reduce sugar and fructose, fruit juice, sodas, high-fructose corn syrup
Limit organ meats, shellfish, and red meat to occasional
Add low-fat dairy, cherries, coffee, these lower uric acid
Lose 5 to 10 percent of body weight if overweight
Drink 2 to 3 liters of water a day to flush urate
low: Low uric acid is usually benign
maintain: Cap fructose at under 25 g per day. Fruit juice, soda, sweetened sauces are the main offenders.
Cap alcohol, especially beer and spirits, at under 5 drinks per week.
Cap red meat at under 3 servings per week. Limit organ meats and shellfish.
Drink 2.5 to 3.5 L water per day.
Eat tart cherries, low-fat dairy, coffee. All lower uric acid.
Aim uric acid under 6.0 mg/dL for men, under 5.0 for women.

ALT (SGPT).desc: Alanine Aminotransferase, an enzyme mostly inside liver cells. Leaks into blood when liver cells are stressed.
ALT (SGPT).why: The most specific routine marker of liver cell damage. Rises with fatty liver, hepatitis, alcohol, and certain medications.
ALT (SGPT).highMeans: High ALT points to liver cell injury. Most common cause today is non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Also: alcohol, viral hepatitis, medications (including some supplements), or muscle injury.
ALT (SGPT).lowMeans: Low ALT can reflect B6 deficiency but is rarely clinically important.
ALT (SGPT).context: Intense exercise can transiently raise ALT because some also comes from muscle.

high: Cut alcohol, even moderate intake keeps ALT elevated
Lose 5 to 10 percent body weight if you carry extra fat around the middle, fatty liver is the top cause
Shift to Mediterranean eating, olive oil, fish, vegetables, whole grains
Cut sugar and fructose, they drive liver fat
Exercise 150 minutes a week plus 2 strength sessions
Review medications and supplements with your doctor, statins, acetaminophen, herbal supplements can raise ALT
Drink 2 to 3 cups of coffee a day if tolerated, coffee lowers ALT
low: Low ALT is usually fine
maintain: Cap alcohol at under 7 drinks per week.
Keep waist circumference under 37 inches (men) or 31.5 inches (women). Visceral fat drives ALT up via fatty liver.
Cut added sugar to under 25 g per day. Fructose is processed in the liver and drives fat accumulation.
Coffee 2 to 3 cups per day.
Aim ALT under 30 U/L. The lab 'normal' upper limit (40 to 55) misses early fatty liver.

AST (SGOT).desc: Aspartate Aminotransferase, an enzyme in liver AND muscle cells. Less specific to the liver than ALT.
AST (SGOT).why: Supports ALT in liver evaluation. AST > ALT (especially 2:1) is a classic pattern of alcoholic liver disease.
AST (SGOT).highMeans: High AST with high ALT suggests liver stress. AST higher than ALT often points to alcohol. AST alone can rise with muscle injury or vigorous exercise.
AST (SGOT).context: Rises with heavy exercise. Avoid intense workouts in the 24-48 hours before testing.

high: Cut alcohol, it is the most common driver
Avoid intense exercise 48 hours before a blood draw, muscle releases AST
Lose weight if fatty liver is the cause, aim for 5 to 10 percent
Review medications with your doctor
low: Low AST is usually fine
maintain: Cap alcohol at 0 to 7 drinks per week. Even moderate drinking elevates liver enzymes within days.
Avoid acetaminophen in doses above 2 g per day, especially with alcohol.
Maintain a healthy bodyweight to prevent fatty liver. Each 1 percent of body fat dropped reduces liver fat by ~0.5 percent.
Coffee 2 to 3 cups per day is liver protective.
Strength train. Muscle work releases small AST bumps but lowers chronic levels.

GGT.desc: Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase, a liver enzyme especially sensitive to alcohol and bile duct issues.
GGT.why: Helps distinguish liver from bone sources of elevated alkaline phosphatase. Very responsive to alcohol intake.
GGT.highMeans: High GGT is often the earliest sign of alcohol-related liver stress. Also rises with bile duct issues, fatty liver, and certain medications.
GGT.lowMeans: Low GGT is not a concern.
GGT.context: Even moderate regular alcohol use can nudge GGT up. Abstaining for 2-4 weeks typically drops it meaningfully.

high: Cut alcohol, GGT is very sensitive to even moderate drinking
Lose weight if fatty liver is suspected
Review medications that stress the liver
Drink coffee (2 to 3 cups) if tolerated, it lowers GGT
low: Low GGT is favorable
maintain: Cap alcohol at under 7 drinks per week. GGT is the most alcohol-sensitive liver enzyme.
Cut sugar-sweetened drinks completely. Fructose elevates GGT.
Avoid unnecessary meds (NSAIDs, statins start) when GGT trends up.
Aim GGT under 30 U/L for adults.

Alk Phosphatase.desc: Alkaline Phosphatase, an enzyme present in liver, bone, intestine, and placenta.
Alk Phosphatase.why: Rises with bile duct issues (liver source) or bone growth/disease (bone source). GGT helps tell which.
Alk Phosphatase.highMeans: High ALP can mean bile duct obstruction, fatty liver, or bone activity (growth in teens, fractures, Paget disease). A normal GGT usually points to bone as the source.
Alk Phosphatase.lowMeans: Low ALP can suggest zinc deficiency, malnutrition, or rare hypophosphatasia.
Alk Phosphatase.context: Adolescents and pregnant women naturally run higher.

high: Check vitamin D, low vitamin D raises alkaline phosphatase
Review bone health, bone turnover can elevate it
Cut alcohol if relevant
low: Ensure adequate zinc, magnesium, and protein
maintain: Maintain vitamin D 40 to 60 ng/mL and calcium intake of 1000 mg per day.
Weight-bearing exercise 3+ times per week supports normal bone turnover.
If trending up alone (no liver enzyme bump), check vitamin D, calcium, and bone health.

Bilirubin Total.desc: A yellow pigment from red blood cell breakdown that's processed by the liver and excreted in bile.
Bilirubin Total.why: Rises when red cells break down faster than normal, or when the liver can't clear it. Very high levels cause jaundice.
Bilirubin Total.highMeans: High bilirubin can be from Gilbert syndrome (benign, genetic, common), hemolysis, or liver/bile duct issues. Gilbert variety is harmless and affects 5-10% of people.
Bilirubin Total.lowMeans: Low bilirubin is not a concern.
Bilirubin Total.context: Fasting, stress, illness, and dehydration can temporarily raise unconjugated bilirubin in Gilbert syndrome.

high: Often Gilbert syndrome and benign, stay well hydrated and eat regularly
Fasting, dehydration, and intense exercise raise it, avoid these the day before labs
Cut alcohol if relevant
low: Low bilirubin is benign
maintain: Mild elevations (Gilbert's syndrome) are benign and even protective.
Stay hydrated. Skipping meals or fasting can transiently raise bilirubin.
Keep alcohol low and avoid hepatotoxic supplement stacks.

Protein Total.desc: The combined amount of albumin and globulin in blood.
Protein Total.why: Screens for liver function, kidney protein loss, dehydration, and abnormal immunoglobulin production.
Protein Total.highMeans: High total protein can be from dehydration, chronic inflammation, or abnormal antibody production (rarely, multiple myeloma).
Protein Total.lowMeans: Low total protein can mean malnutrition, liver disease, kidney protein loss (nephrotic syndrome), or chronic illness.
Protein Total.context: Always interpret alongside albumin and globulin, they drive the total.

high: Ensure good hydration through the day, dehydration concentrates proteins
low: Increase protein intake to about 1 to 1.2 g per kg body weight
Include eggs, fish, dairy, legumes, and lean meat at each meal
maintain: Hit 1.2 to 1.6 g protein per kg bodyweight daily.
Stay hydrated.

Albumin.desc: The main protein in blood, made by the liver. Holds fluid inside your vessels and carries hormones, drugs, and calcium.
Albumin.why: A marker of liver synthesis and nutritional status. Low albumin is a strong prognostic signal across many illnesses.
Albumin.highMeans: High albumin is almost always dehydration.
Albumin.lowMeans: Low albumin can be from liver disease, protein loss in urine or gut, severe inflammation, or malnutrition.
Albumin.context: Albumin has a long half-life (~20 days), so it responds to changes slowly.

high: Usually just dehydration, drink water steadily
low: Raise protein intake to 1 to 1.2 g per kg body weight
Include eggs, fish, dairy, legumes, and lean meat at each meal
Address any gut issues that may impair absorption
maintain: Hit 1.2 to 1.6 g protein per kg bodyweight per day. For 80 kg = 96 to 128 g protein daily.
Distribute protein across 3 to 4 meals (25 to 40 g per meal).
Stay hydrated. Dehydration falsely raises albumin.
Strength train. Liver synthesis of albumin tracks with anabolic state.

Globulin.desc: A group of proteins including antibodies (immunoglobulins) and carrier proteins.
Globulin.why: Helps assess immune activity and liver function. High globulin can indicate chronic inflammation or abnormal antibody production.
Globulin.highMeans: High globulin often reflects chronic infection, autoimmune disease, liver disease, or (rarely) multiple myeloma.
Globulin.lowMeans: Low globulin may suggest immune deficiency or severe malnutrition.
Globulin.context: Calculated as Total Protein minus Albumin in many labs.

high: Often reflects chronic inflammation, add omega-3, lower sugar, exercise, sleep
low: Ensure balanced protein intake
maintain: Keep inflammation low (see hs-CRP plan).
If persistently elevated, ask about serum protein electrophoresis to rule out monoclonal gammopathy.

A/G Ratio.desc: Albumin divided by Globulin, a ratio that helps flag shifts in protein fractions.
A/G Ratio.why: A high or low ratio can point toward specific problems even when total protein looks normal.
A/G Ratio.highMeans: High A/G ratio can be from low globulin (some immune deficiencies) or certain genetic conditions, often benign.
A/G Ratio.lowMeans: Low A/G ratio suggests either low albumin or high globulin, worth looking at both proteins separately.
A/G Ratio.context: Ratio is most useful in conjunction with the individual values, not alone.

high: Keep protein intake steady and stay hydrated
low: Work on lowering inflammation, Mediterranean diet, exercise, sleep, weight loss
maintain: Drive both sides. Maintain albumin with adequate protein, control globulin by keeping chronic inflammation in check.

Sodium.desc: The primary electrolyte outside your cells. Tightly regulated by kidneys and hormones.
Sodium.why: Sodium imbalances cause neurological symptoms (confusion, seizures when severe). Small deviations rarely matter.
Sodium.highMeans: High sodium (hypernatremia) is almost always dehydration or inadequate water intake.
Sodium.lowMeans: Low sodium (hyponatremia) can be from overhydration, certain medications (diuretics, SSRIs), heart/kidney/liver disease, or hormonal issues.
Sodium.context: Tightly regulated, even small deviations (2-3 mmol/L) can matter in the right clinical picture.

high: Drink more water, the most common cause is dehydration
Cut back on very salty foods if intake is extreme
low: Avoid over-drinking plain water during endurance events, add electrolytes
Review diuretic or antidepressant medications with your doctor
maintain: Drink to thirst. Most sodium issues are hydration related.
Cap added salt at 5 to 6 g per day if blood pressure is borderline.

Potassium.desc: The main electrolyte inside your cells. Essential for heart rhythm and muscle function.
Potassium.why: Even small abnormalities can affect heart rhythm. Watched carefully in patients on kidney or heart medications.
Potassium.highMeans: High potassium (hyperkalemia) can be from kidney issues, certain medications (ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics), or a hemolyzed blood sample.
Potassium.lowMeans: Low potassium (hypokalemia) usually comes from diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea, or magnesium deficiency.
Potassium.context: A hemolyzed sample (red cells broken during draw) falsely raises potassium. Repeat before acting.

high: If you take potassium supplements or salt substitutes, stop and recheck
Review ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and potassium-sparing diuretics with your doctor
low: Add bananas, potatoes with skin, beans, leafy greens, avocado, tomato
Limit alcohol, it drops potassium
Review diuretic medications with your doctor
maintain: Eat 4 to 5 servings of potassium-rich foods per day. Banana, avocado, potato, sweet potato, beans, leafy greens, salmon, yogurt.
Aim 4000 mg per day intake. Most people get 2000 to 2500.
Avoid potassium supplements unless prescribed. Food sources only.

Chloride.desc: The partner of sodium in maintaining fluid balance and acid-base status.
Chloride.why: Supports interpretation of acid-base problems and sodium/water imbalances.
Chloride.highMeans: High chloride usually tracks with high sodium or metabolic acidosis.
Chloride.lowMeans: Low chloride usually tracks with low sodium or can suggest vomiting (loss of stomach acid).

high: Stay hydrated and reduce very high salt intake
low: Usually tracks sodium, address hydration and medication causes
maintain: Stay hydrated, cap added salt at 5 to 6 g per day.

Bicarbonate.desc: The body's main chemical buffer that keeps blood pH stable. Sometimes labeled CO2 on labs.
Bicarbonate.why: Detects acid-base problems. Low bicarbonate = metabolic acidosis; high = metabolic alkalosis.
Bicarbonate.highMeans: High bicarbonate (metabolic alkalosis) can be from vomiting, diuretic use, or respiratory compensation for lung disease.
Bicarbonate.lowMeans: Low bicarbonate (metabolic acidosis) can be from diabetic ketoacidosis, kidney disease, severe diarrhea, or certain toxic ingestions.
Bicarbonate.context: Interpret with a full metabolic panel. Severely abnormal values need urgent evaluation.

high: Review diuretic use and vomiting history with your doctor
low: Stay hydrated, address any chronic diarrhea, keep blood sugar under control
maintain: Eat 5+ servings of vegetables and fruit per day for the alkalinizing load.
Don't overdo high-intensity exercise without recovery.

Calcium.desc: The mineral critical for bones, muscle contraction, heart rhythm, and nerve signaling.
Calcium.why: Tightly regulated by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D. Abnormal levels cause neurological and heart symptoms.
Calcium.highMeans: High calcium (hypercalcemia) can be from overactive parathyroid, certain cancers, high vitamin D, or dehydration.
Calcium.lowMeans: Low calcium can be from low vitamin D, kidney disease, or low parathyroid function. Low albumin falsely lowers total calcium (correct using ionized calcium or corrected calcium formula).
Calcium.context: Low albumin can falsely lower the total calcium reading. Ask for ionized calcium if albumin is abnormal.

high: Review vitamin D and calcium supplementation, over-supplementing is a common cause
Drink more water and keep active
low: Increase dairy, fortified plant milks, leafy greens, sardines, almonds
Ensure vitamin D is adequate, calcium is not absorbed without it
maintain: Hit 1000 mg calcium per day from food. 1 cup yogurt = 300 mg, 1 oz hard cheese = 200 mg, 1 cup cooked kale = 180 mg, 3 oz canned salmon with bones = 180 mg.
Keep vitamin D between 40 and 60 ng/mL for absorption.
Weight-bearing exercise (running, jumping, lifting) 3 to 4 times per week.
Skip calcium supplements if you eat dairy. Supplements raise vascular calcification risk; food calcium does not.

Magnesium.desc: A mineral involved in over 300 enzyme reactions, including energy metabolism, muscle relaxation, and sleep quality.
Magnesium.why: Often deficient with restricted diets, alcohol use, or chronic stress. Low magnesium worsens low potassium and low calcium.
Magnesium.highMeans: High magnesium is uncommon, usually from supplements or kidney disease.
Magnesium.lowMeans: Low magnesium is common and contributes to muscle cramps, poor sleep, migraines, and arrhythmias. Often worsens low potassium.
Magnesium.context: Serum magnesium underestimates true deficiency, it only reflects 1% of total body magnesium.

high: Review magnesium supplements or laxatives, cut or reduce dose
low: Add pumpkin seeds, almonds, cashews, dark chocolate, black beans, spinach
Cut back on alcohol, it depletes magnesium
Consider 200 to 400 mg magnesium glycinate at bedtime if dietary intake is low
maintain: Eat 400 mg magnesium per day from food. 1 oz pumpkin seeds = 150 mg, 1 oz dark chocolate (85 percent+) = 65 mg, 1 cup cooked spinach = 160 mg, 1 oz almonds = 80 mg, 1 cup black beans = 120 mg.
If diet falls short, supplement 200 to 400 mg magnesium glycinate at night. Helps sleep too.
Avoid magnesium oxide. Cheap, poorly absorbed, just causes loose stools.
Aim serum magnesium 2.0 to 2.4 mg/dL. The lab range starts at 1.7 but optimal is higher.

Serum Iron.desc: The amount of iron bound to transferrin and circulating in blood right now.
Serum Iron.why: Part of a full iron panel but fluctuates a lot, most useful with ferritin, TIBC, and transferrin saturation.
Serum Iron.highMeans: High serum iron can reflect recent iron supplementation, a high-iron meal, or (rarely) hemochromatosis (iron overload).
Serum Iron.lowMeans: Low serum iron can mean iron deficiency, chronic inflammation, or blood loss.
Serum Iron.context: Diurnal variation is large, draw in the morning and fasting for consistency. Single readings are unreliable.

high: Cut red meat to under 2 servings per week.
Stop iron supplements and check supplement labels for iron.
Donate blood every 8 to 12 weeks if persistent and you qualify.
Cook in non-iron cookware.
If transferrin saturation is also high (above 45 percent) and ferritin is high, screen for HFE gene mutations (hemochromatosis).
low: Eat 4 to 6 oz red meat or dark poultry 3 to 4 times per week, oysters or sardines weekly.
Add 1 cup cooked lentils, beans, or chickpeas daily, plus 2 tbsp pumpkin seeds.
Pair plant iron with vitamin C in the same meal (bell pepper, citrus, kiwi).
Skip coffee and tea within 60 to 90 minutes of iron meals.
If ferritin is also low, take 25 to 50 mg ferrous bisglycinate every other day with vitamin C. Every-other-day dosing absorbs better than daily.
maintain: Eat heme iron 3 to 4 times per week. 4 to 6 oz lean red meat (beef, lamb), liver once every 2 weeks, oysters or sardines, dark turkey or chicken thigh.
Add plant iron daily. 1 cup cooked lentils or chickpeas, 2 tbsp pumpkin seeds, half a cup of cooked spinach, 1 cup quinoa.
Pair non-heme iron with 50 to 100 mg vitamin C in the same meal. Bell pepper, citrus, kiwi, strawberries, broccoli.
Skip coffee and tea within 60 to 90 minutes of iron-rich meals. Tannins block absorption by 50 to 70 percent.
Avoid taking calcium supplements within 2 hours of iron-rich meals.
Recheck iron panel yearly along with ferritin, TIBC, and transferrin saturation.

Ferritin.desc: The body's main iron storage protein. Ferritin levels reflect iron reserves in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.
Ferritin.why: The single best marker of iron stores. Low ferritin = true iron deficiency, even if Hemoglobin is still normal.
Ferritin.highMeans: High ferritin usually reflects inflammation, chronic disease, liver disease, or heavy alcohol use. Very high levels (>1000) suggest iron overload.
Ferritin.lowMeans: Low ferritin means iron deficiency, even if you're not yet anemic, symptoms like fatigue, brain fog, hair loss, and cold intolerance are common.
Ferritin.context: Ferritin rises with inflammation, so a 'normal' ferritin with active inflammation can mask true iron deficiency. Interpret with hs-CRP.

high: Cut alcohol completely for 8 to 12 weeks and recheck.
Cut red meat to under 2 servings per week, stop any iron supplements.
Address inflammation: Mediterranean diet, sleep, exercise. Ferritin rises with inflammation even when iron stores are fine.
If ferritin stays above 300 to 400 with high transferrin saturation, ask for HFE gene testing for hemochromatosis.
low: Eat 4 to 6 oz red meat or dark poultry 3 to 4 times per week.
Take 25 to 50 mg ferrous bisglycinate every other day with 500 mg vitamin C, on an empty stomach if tolerated. Every-other-day dosing beats daily.
Take iron at least 2 hours away from coffee, tea, calcium, dairy, and zinc.
Address blood loss sources (heavy periods, GI bleeding, frequent blood donation).
Recheck ferritin in 8 to 12 weeks. Aim 70 to 200 ng/mL, not just 'in range'.
maintain: Anchor 3 to 4 weekly meals with iron-rich proteins. 4 to 6 oz beef, lamb, dark poultry, or 1 cup cooked legumes.
Eat oysters, mussels, or sardines once or twice a month for high bioavailable iron.
Cook acidic dishes (tomato sauce, chili) in cast iron. Adds 2 to 5 mg of iron per serving.
If menstruating, prioritize iron the week of and after the period to replace 15 to 25 mg of lost iron.
Address blood loss sources early (heavy periods, bleeding gums, GI symptoms). Even slow loss drops ferritin within months.
Recheck ferritin yearly. Aim 70 to 200 ng/mL for an active adult, not just 'in range'.

TIBC.desc: Total Iron Binding Capacity, how much iron transferrin (the main iron transport protein) could theoretically carry.
TIBC.why: TIBC rises in iron deficiency (body makes more transferrin to grab scarce iron) and falls in inflammation.
TIBC.lowMeans: Low TIBC suggests chronic inflammation, liver disease, or malnutrition.
TIBC.context: Interpret alongside serum iron and ferritin.

high: Suggests iron need, add iron-rich foods and vitamin C
low: Usually reflects inflammation or iron overload, focus on anti-inflammatory habits
maintain: Keep iron intake balanced from the foods listed under iron and ferritin.
Limit alcohol to less than 7 drinks per week. Heavy drinking distorts transferrin metabolism.
Manage chronic inflammation with whole foods, sleep, and exercise.

Transferrin Saturation.desc: The percentage of transferrin (the iron taxi) that's actually carrying iron. Calculated as Serum Iron ÷ TIBC.
Transferrin Saturation.why: Cross-checks iron status. Saturation <20% supports iron deficiency; >45% can suggest iron overload.
Transferrin Saturation.highMeans: High saturation (>45%) can suggest hereditary hemochromatosis, especially if ferritin is also elevated.
Transferrin Saturation.context: Must be drawn fasting and not after iron supplementation.

high: Cut iron supplements and heavy red meat
Check ferritin, if also high, screen for hemochromatosis
low: Boost iron intake and pair with vitamin C
maintain: Eat heme iron 2 to 3 times per week, plant iron daily, and include vitamin C at meals.
Donate blood once a year if your saturation runs 40 to 45 percent and ferritin is high-normal.
If you have a family history of hemochromatosis, ask your doctor about HFE gene testing.

TSH.desc: Thyroid Stimulating Hormone, released by the pituitary to tell the thyroid how hard to work.
TSH.why: The single best screening test for thyroid disease. TSH moves opposite to thyroid hormone levels.
TSH.highMeans: High TSH means your pituitary is telling the thyroid to work harder, usually because thyroid hormone levels are low (hypothyroidism).
TSH.lowMeans: Low TSH means the pituitary is dialing back, either because thyroid hormone is too high (hyperthyroidism) or because of pituitary issues or certain medications.
TSH.context: TSH has diurnal rhythm, slightly higher in the morning. Test at the same time of day if tracking trends.

high: Get iodine from iodized salt, seafood, seaweed, dairy, eggs
Add selenium from 2 to 3 Brazil nuts a day
Ask your doctor to check anti-TPO antibodies if TSH is over 4
Reduce chronic stress and prioritize sleep
low: Review any thyroid medication or iodine supplements with your doctor
Manage stress and get 7 to 9 hours of sleep
maintain: Get 150 mcg iodine per day. Half a teaspoon iodized salt, or 1 to 2 servings of seafood per week.
Get 100 to 200 mcg selenium per day. 2 Brazil nuts = 200 mcg.
Maintain bodyweight. Big weight swings disrupt thyroid signaling.
Sleep 7 to 9 hours. Sleep deprivation raises TSH.
Manage stress. Chronic cortisol elevation suppresses T4 to T3 conversion.
Aim TSH 1.0 to 2.0 mIU/L for optimal energy and metabolism, even though 0.4 to 4.5 is 'normal'.

Free T4.desc: The unbound, active form of thyroxine, one of the two main thyroid hormones.
Free T4.why: Confirms what TSH suggests. High TSH + low Free T4 = clear hypothyroidism.
Free T4.highMeans: High Free T4 with suppressed TSH suggests hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid).
Free T4.lowMeans: Low Free T4 with high TSH confirms hypothyroidism.
Free T4.context: Always interpret with TSH, they tell the full story together.

high: Review any thyroid medication or supplements with your doctor
low: Ensure iodine and selenium are adequate, see thyroid diet tips
maintain: Get 150 mcg iodine and 100 to 200 mcg selenium daily.
Avoid restrictive low-calorie diets long term. T4 drops within weeks.
Aim Free T4 in upper third of range.

Free T3.desc: The unbound, active form of triiodothyronine, the most metabolically active thyroid hormone.
Free T3.why: Useful when Free T4 is normal but symptoms suggest thyroid dysfunction. Also used to confirm hyperthyroidism.
Free T3.lowMeans: Low Free T3 with low/normal Free T4 can suggest Euthyroid Sick Syndrome (low T3 during illness) or peripheral conversion issues.
Free T3.context: Not used as a primary screen, TSH and Free T4 come first.

high: Review thyroid medication and stimulants with your doctor
low: Address selenium and zinc intake, both convert T4 to T3
Reduce chronic under-eating or over-exercising, both suppress T3
maintain: Eat enough carbs (at least 100 g per day for most active adults). T3 conversion drops on chronic low-carb.
Selenium 100 to 200 mcg per day supports T4 to T3 conversion.
Manage cortisol with sleep, walking, and stress practices.
Aim Free T3 in upper third of range.

Vitamin D (25-OH).desc: 25-hydroxy Vitamin D, the storage form of vitamin D and the best marker of vitamin D status.
Vitamin D (25-OH).why: Supports bone health, immune function, mood, and testosterone. Deficiency is very common, especially in darker-skinned people and those who spend most of the day indoors.
Vitamin D (25-OH).highMeans: Very high vitamin D (>100 ng/mL) can cause high calcium. Almost always from over-supplementation.
Vitamin D (25-OH).lowMeans: Low vitamin D (<30 ng/mL) is common and linked to fatigue, poor sleep, bone loss, low testosterone, and worse immune function.
Vitamin D (25-OH).context: Different labs report in ng/mL or nmol/L. To convert nmol/L to ng/mL divide by 2.5.

high: Reduce or pause vitamin D supplementation and retest in 2 to 3 months
low: Get 15 to 20 minutes of midday sun on arms and face most days
Eat fatty fish (salmon, sardines) twice a week and egg yolks
Supplement 2000 IU D3 daily with a fatty meal, 4000 IU if under 20 ng per mL
Ensure magnesium is adequate, it is needed to activate vitamin D
maintain: Get 15 to 30 minutes midday sun on arms and legs 4 to 5 times per week (no SPF for that window).
If you live above latitude 35 or work indoors, supplement 2000 to 4000 IU vitamin D3 daily, taken with a meal containing fat.
Add 100 to 200 mcg vitamin K2 (MK-7) daily to direct calcium to bones not arteries.
Aim 40 to 60 ng/mL year-round, recheck after 3 months of any dose change.

Vitamin B12.desc: A water-soluble vitamin essential for nerve function, red cell production, and energy.
Vitamin B12.why: Deficiency causes fatigue, brain fog, tingling, and eventually anemia. Common in vegans and in anyone with reduced stomach acid (PPI users, elderly).
Vitamin B12.highMeans: High B12 is usually from supplementation, rarely concerning. Very high levels without supplementation can occasionally signal liver disease or certain cancers.
Vitamin B12.lowMeans: Low B12 (<300 pg/mL) can cause neurological symptoms even before anemia develops. Levels 300-500 are borderline and worth rechecking with methylmalonic acid.
Vitamin B12.context: Vegans, vegetarians, and long-term PPI users should check B12 routinely. Methylmalonic acid is more sensitive than B12 for borderline cases.

high: Review B12 supplements, pause and retest
low: Eat fish, eggs, dairy, and meat regularly, or take 500 to 1000 mcg methylcobalamin daily if vegetarian or vegan
Check for chronic acid-blocker or metformin use, both reduce B12 absorption
maintain: Eat animal protein 3 to 5 times per week. 3 oz beef = 2.4 mcg, 3 oz salmon = 4.8 mcg, 1 cup yogurt = 1.4 mcg, 2 eggs = 1.2 mcg.
If vegetarian, supplement 500 to 1000 mcg methylcobalamin daily, sublingual.
Aim serum B12 above 500 pg/mL. The lab 'normal' starts at 200 but neurological symptoms appear well above that.
If on metformin or PPIs long-term, supplement and recheck yearly.

hs-CRP.desc: High-sensitivity C-Reactive Protein, a marker of inflammation in the body.
hs-CRP.why: Used to assess cardiovascular risk and track chronic inflammation. Low-grade elevation predicts heart disease independent of cholesterol.
hs-CRP.highMeans: Above 3 mg/L suggests high cardiovascular risk or active inflammation somewhere. Very high (>10) usually means acute infection or injury, retest after recovery.
hs-CRP.lowMeans: Low hs-CRP is favorable and suggests low inflammation.
hs-CRP.context: Temporarily rises with any infection, injury, or intense exercise. Retest 2-4 weeks after any acute illness.

high: Eat Mediterranean style, olive oil, fatty fish, nuts, legumes, lots of vegetables and berries
Exercise 150 minutes a week plus 2 strength sessions
Drop 5 to 10 percent of body weight if BMI is above 25, fat drives CRP
Sleep 7 to 9 hours, short sleep elevates CRP within a week
Quit smoking and cap alcohol at one drink a day
Brush and floss daily, gum disease keeps CRP elevated
low: Low CRP is favorable
maintain: Eat Mediterranean style. Vegetables and fruit at every meal, olive oil as primary fat, fish 2 times per week, beans and whole grains daily, low red meat.
Train 150 min per week. Exercise lowers CRP independent of weight.
Sleep 7 to 9 hours. Skimping raises IL-6 and CRP the next day.
Floss daily. Periodontal inflammation drives systemic CRP.
Cap alcohol at under 7 drinks per week.
Aim hs-CRP under 1.0 mg/L. Anything above 2 is a yellow flag.

ASO.desc: Anti-Streptolysin O, an antibody produced after a streptococcal infection.
ASO.why: Used to confirm recent strep infection, especially when investigating rheumatic fever or post-strep glomerulonephritis.
ASO.highMeans: Elevated ASO suggests a recent strep infection. Peaks 3-5 weeks after infection, then gradually declines.
ASO.lowMeans: Low ASO is the norm and indicates no recent strep exposure.
ASO.context: A single high ASO is less meaningful than a rising titer over 2-4 weeks.

high: Recent strep exposure is typical, complete any antibiotic course prescribed
If elevation persists, a follow-up with your doctor is reasonable
low: No action
maintain: Address recurrent strep infections promptly.
Trends matter more than a single value.

Rheumatoid Factor.desc: An autoantibody that targets your own antibodies. Elevated in rheumatoid arthritis and some other conditions.
Rheumatoid Factor.why: Screening test for rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases. Not specific, elevated in 5-10% of healthy people.
Rheumatoid Factor.highMeans: Elevated RF supports rheumatoid arthritis in the right clinical context (joint pain, stiffness). Also elevated in some infections and other autoimmune conditions.
Rheumatoid Factor.lowMeans: Low RF is reassuring but doesn't completely rule out RA.
Rheumatoid Factor.context: Anti-CCP antibodies are more specific for RA than RF.

high: Discuss autoimmune screening (anti-CCP, ANA) with your doctor if joints are involved
Eat anti-inflammatory, Mediterranean style, add omega-3
Quit smoking if relevant
low: No action
maintain: Mediterranean diet, regular training, vitamin D 40 to 60 ng/mL.
Address joint symptoms early with a rheumatologist if persistent.

CRP (Quantitative).desc: C-Reactive Protein, standard sensitivity, a general inflammation marker.
CRP (Quantitative).why: Rises within hours of infection, injury, or active inflammation. Standard CRP is good for detecting acute inflammation.
CRP (Quantitative).highMeans: High CRP signals active inflammation somewhere. Causes range from infection to autoimmune flares to injury.
CRP (Quantitative).context: If you're investigating cardiovascular risk, use hs-CRP instead, it measures the same molecule with more precision at low levels.

high: Same playbook as hs-CRP, Mediterranean diet, exercise, sleep, weight
Address any active infection or dental issues
low: Low CRP is favorable
maintain: Same as hs-CRP. Mediterranean diet, 150 min per week of training, 7 to 9 hours sleep, low alcohol, dental hygiene.

CPK / CK.desc: Creatine Phosphokinase (also called Creatine Kinase), an enzyme inside muscle cells that leaks into blood when muscle is damaged.
CPK / CK.why: Rises with muscle injury, intense exercise, certain medications (especially statins), and rare muscle diseases. Also a heart attack marker when broken down into subtypes.
CPK / CK.highMeans: High CPK most commonly reflects intense exercise in the past 24-72 hours. Statin-related muscle damage, muscle trauma, prolonged sitting pressure, and rare muscle disorders can also raise it. Heart attack raises CK-MB subtype specifically.
CPK / CK.lowMeans: Low CPK is rarely meaningful. May be seen with low muscle mass or certain autoimmune conditions.
CPK / CK.context: Skip heavy exercise for 48-72 hours before testing for a clean baseline. Eccentric exercise (downhill running, heavy lifting) can quintuple CPK for several days.

high: Skip intense workouts for 48 to 72 hours before a blood draw
Hydrate well around workouts
Review statins with your doctor if you also have muscle aches
low: Usually benign, add strength training
maintain: If you train hard, CK will run elevated. That is normal in athletes.
Stay hydrated, especially around heavy training.
If extremely elevated (above 5x upper limit) without obvious training reason, slow down and recheck.

CK-MB.desc: The heart-muscle-specific subtype of CPK. Normally makes up a small fraction of total CK.
CK-MB.why: Historically used to diagnose heart attacks. Now largely replaced by troponin, but still reported.
CK-MB.highMeans: Elevated CK-MB with chest pain suggests cardiac muscle injury (heart attack). Can also rise with severe skeletal muscle damage.
CK-MB.context: Troponin is now the preferred marker for heart attacks, CK-MB is less specific. The ratio of CK-MB to total CK matters: >5% suggests cardiac origin.

high: If mildly raised after heavy exercise it can be benign, rest 48 to 72 hours and retest
If raised without a clear cause, see a doctor promptly
low: No action
maintain: Should be a small fraction of total CK in healthy people.
If elevated, evaluate cardiac causes.

Troponin-I.desc: A protein released when heart muscle is damaged. The single most specific marker of heart attack.
Troponin-I.why: Any detectable elevation is concerning in the right clinical context. Ultra-sensitive assays can detect very small amounts.
Troponin-I.highMeans: Elevated troponin strongly suggests heart muscle injury, heart attack, myocarditis, or severe strain (marathon, pulmonary embolism). Always treat as urgent unless explained by a clear non-cardiac cause.
Troponin-I.lowMeans: Undetectable or low troponin is reassuring and essentially rules out acute heart attack.
Troponin-I.context: Must be drawn at least 3-6 hours after chest pain onset for full sensitivity. Sometimes repeated at 3 and 6 hours.

high: Seek urgent medical care, elevated troponin can signal heart muscle injury
low: No action
maintain: Drive cardiovascular health. Lipids on target, blood pressure under 120/80, HbA1c under 5.4, 150 min training per week.
Any detectable troponin in an asymptomatic person warrants follow-up.

Testosterone Total.desc: The primary male sex hormone. Drives muscle mass, energy, libido, and mood. Also present in smaller amounts in women.
Testosterone Total.why: Low levels in men cause fatigue, low libido, depressed mood, reduced muscle mass, and worsened metabolic health.
Testosterone Total.highMeans: Very high testosterone in men usually means exogenous supplementation (TRT or anabolic steroids).
Testosterone Total.lowMeans: Low testosterone causes fatigue, low libido, poor sleep, reduced muscle, and irritability. Drivers include obesity, poor sleep, low vitamin D, and aging (1-2% decline per year after 30).
Testosterone Total.context: Must be drawn in the morning (7-10 AM), fasting, after 8+ hours of sleep. A single low reading needs confirmation on a second morning draw.

high: Review any testosterone or steroid supplements with your doctor
low: Prioritize sleep, 7 to 9 hours, deep sleep is when testosterone is made
Do 2 to 4 strength sessions a week with compound lifts
Lose 5 to 10 percent body weight if overweight, fat tissue converts testosterone to estrogen
Ensure adequate zinc (oysters, beef, pumpkin seeds) and vitamin D
Limit alcohol to 0 to 3 drinks a week
Manage chronic stress, cortisol suppresses testosterone
maintain: Sleep 7 to 9 hours. Each hour under 7 drops testosterone 10 to 15 percent.
Strength train 3 to 4 times per week. Compound lifts (squat, deadlift, press, row).
Eat 0.4 to 0.5 g fat per kg bodyweight from olive oil, eggs, fatty fish, nuts. Very low fat diets crash testosterone.
Get sun on skin midday for vitamin D, target 40 to 60 ng/mL.
Hold bodyweight within 5 percent of optimal. Excess body fat aromatizes testosterone to estrogen.
Cap alcohol at under 7 drinks per week.
Aim total testosterone 600 to 900 ng/dL for an active adult man, free T 15 to 25 pg/mL.

FSH.desc: Follicle Stimulating Hormone, released by the pituitary to regulate testicular function (in men) or ovarian function (in women).
FSH.why: In men, FSH supports sperm production. High FSH with low testosterone suggests primary testicular failure.
FSH.highMeans: High FSH with low testosterone in men suggests the testes aren't responding, primary hypogonadism. In women, it signals reduced ovarian function or menopause.
FSH.lowMeans: Low FSH can suggest pituitary issues or, in men, exogenous testosterone use shutting down the HPG axis.
FSH.context: Always interpreted with LH and testosterone (men) or estradiol (women).

high: Discuss with a doctor, especially if fertility is a goal
low: Discuss with a doctor, look for pituitary or lifestyle causes
maintain: Sleep 7 to 9 hours, manage stress, maintain bodyweight.
If trying to conceive, recheck FSH and LH together with testosterone.

LH.desc: Luteinizing Hormone, released by the pituitary to trigger testosterone production (in men) or ovulation (in women).
LH.why: Helps classify the cause of low testosterone in men: high LH = testicular issue; low LH = pituitary issue.
LH.highMeans: High LH with low testosterone in men indicates primary hypogonadism (testicular failure).
LH.lowMeans: Low LH with low testosterone suggests secondary hypogonadism (pituitary/hypothalamic issue) or exogenous testosterone use.
LH.context: Secreted in pulses, so single readings have significant variability.

high: Pair with FSH and testosterone for context, discuss with an endocrinologist
low: Review training load, sleep, and nutrition, severe calorie deficits suppress LH
maintain: Same as FSH. Sleep, stress, bodyweight, and avoid anabolic supplements that suppress the HPG axis.

PSA Total.desc: Prostate-Specific Antigen, a protein made by the prostate. Elevated levels can suggest prostate issues.
PSA Total.why: Used to screen for prostate cancer and monitor prostate conditions. Interpretation depends strongly on age.
PSA Total.highMeans: Elevated PSA can be from prostate cancer, benign prostate enlargement (BPH), prostatitis, recent ejaculation, or a recent prostate exam. Free PSA ratio helps distinguish cancer from benign causes.
PSA Total.lowMeans: Low PSA is favorable and suggests low prostate cancer risk.
PSA Total.context: Avoid ejaculation, vigorous cycling, and prostate exams for 48 hours before testing. PSA rises slightly with age, age-adjusted ranges exist.

high: Avoid ejaculation, cycling, and prostate exams in the 48 hours before the test
Cut alcohol, add tomatoes, cruciferous vegetables, and omega-3
Follow up with a repeat PSA and prostate exam if values stay elevated
low: Low PSA is favorable
maintain: Eat 4 to 6 servings of cruciferous vegetables per week (broccoli, cauliflower, kale, brussels sprouts).
Add 2 tbsp ground flaxseed daily.
Cooked tomatoes 2 to 3 times per week for lycopene.
Strength train 2 to 3 times per week, 150 min cardio.
Cap red meat at 3 servings per week, especially charred or processed.
Recheck PSA yearly after age 45 and discuss any rapid rise (over 0.75 ng/mL per year) with a urologist.

Zinc (Serum).desc: An essential trace mineral involved in immune function, wound healing, taste, smell, and testosterone production.
Zinc (Serum).why: Deficiency is common with restrictive diets, GI disorders, heavy alcohol use, or aging. Symptoms include frequent infections, slow wound healing, hair loss, and low libido.
Zinc (Serum).highMeans: High serum zinc is almost always from supplementation. Long-term high intake can cause copper deficiency.
Zinc (Serum).lowMeans: Low zinc causes immune problems, slow healing, taste loss, and can lower testosterone.
Zinc (Serum).context: Take supplements with food, on an empty stomach zinc often causes nausea. Zinc and copper compete for absorption, so balance matters long-term.

high: Review zinc supplements, stop and retest
low: Eat oysters, beef, pumpkin seeds, cashews, lentils, eggs, and dairy
Limit alcohol and heavy iron supplementation, both reduce zinc absorption
Consider 15 to 25 mg zinc with dinner if intake is low
maintain: Eat 11 to 15 mg zinc per day. 6 medium oysters = 32 mg, 3 oz beef = 7 mg, 1 oz pumpkin seeds = 2 mg, 1 cup chickpeas = 2.5 mg.
If you supplement, cap at 25 to 30 mg elemental zinc and pair with 2 mg copper to avoid copper depletion.
Don't take zinc with iron or calcium at the same time. Take separated by 2 hours.
